title: Time matters: temporal concepts in developmental science
abstract: Developmental science typically emphasizes two key dimensions of data: variables and persons. The third dimension – time – has received comparatively less attention. This article highlights the critical role of timing in developmental research and encourages to utilize known dynamic concepts of development in research questions more often, such as the life stage principle, the phase transition perspective, and dynamic concepts derived from puberty research. The life stage perspective emphasizes how age-graded transitions and social timing shape development. The phase transition perspective focuses on discrete shifts or life changes that can influence mechanisms of individual functioning. The pubertal timing perspective provides concepts that help capturing variability in the onset and progression of developmental changes. To illustrate the utility of these perspectives, I present empirical evidence primarily drawn from acculturation research. This field is particularly informative for understanding dynamic developmental processes because it highlights the co-action and interaction between developmental and acculturation-related change, particularly among immigrant and minoritized youth. Adding timing as a central analytic dimension of analysis and practice promises to improve intervention designs, can enhance predictions of adaptation, and supports positive developmental trajectories across diverse contexts.
